title: Exploring Disinformation: The interplay of exposure, trust, and sharing
screen_reason: Nationally balanced online panel survey of 3,240 Czech adults (June 2023). Respondents were shown seven real disinformation narratives circulating in the Czech information environment and asked, for each, whether they had encountered it and whether they had shared it. The paper reports shares of respondents who recognised at least one / five or more narratives (self-reported exposure = RECALL exposure) and shares who reported sharing at least one (RECALL sharing). Belief/trust outcomes and the discernment score are NOT extracted (belief is explicitly out of scope).

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; narratives circulating in Czech online media and social networks, asked in an online survey
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported having previously encountered at least one of seven political disinformation narratives
estimates.value_raw: 2131/3240 = 65.8% (paper: 'those who had encountered at least one disinformation item (N = 2131)'; complementary statement: '34.2 % reported not recognizing any of the seven disinformation narratives')
estimates.denominator: 3,240 Czech-speaking adults aged 16+ in a quota-balanced national online panel (final analytic sample)
estimates.definition: Respondent indicated, for at least one of the seven presented disinformation narratives, that they had encountered it before
estimates.misinfo_def: “information that is (i) false, (ii) communicated as true, and (iii) intentionally communicated as true in order to influence people’s beliefs or behavior” (Kwek et al., 2023)
estimates.source_quote: Exposure to disinformation. Approximately one third of participants (34.2 %) reported not recognizing any of the seven disinformation narratives presented. ... Among those who had encountered at least one disinformation item (N = 2131), the majority (86 %) did not share any
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Seven disinformation narratives and three verified true news items selected by media experts on the basis of demonstrable presence/popularity in Czech online media, polarising potential and thematic relevance; the true news items were verified through an independent fact-checking procedure. No inter-rater reliability reported for narrative selection.
estimates.moderator_quote: Seven disinformation narratives and three verified true news items were selected by media experts based on their relevance and salience in the Czech information environment at the time of data collection. ... (e.g., Russian aggression in Ukraine, EU regulation, US military presence in Czechia).
estimates.notes: Exposure is narrative-specific recognition of seven curated real narratives, not a generic 'have you seen misinformation' item, so the level depends on which narratives were chosen (the authors flag this as a limitation). The 65.8% is the exact part/whole of two verbatim numbers with the same denominator (2131 of 3240); the paper itself states only the complement (34.2% unexposed).

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; narratives circulating in Czech online media and social networks, asked in an online survey
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported having previously encountered five or more of the seven political disinformation narratives
estimates.value_raw: 6.5% of 3,240 recognized five or more of seven narratives
estimates.denominator: 3,240 Czech-speaking adults aged 16+ in a quota-balanced national online panel
estimates.definition: Respondent reported previously encountering 5, 6 or 7 of the seven presented disinformation narratives ('Highly exposed' category)
estimates.misinfo_def: “information that is (i) false, (ii) communicated as true, and (iii) intentionally communicated as true in order to influence people’s beliefs or behavior” (Kwek et al., 2023)
estimates.source_quote: In contrast, 6.5 % recognized five or more.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Narratives selected by media experts; no reliability statistic reported for selection.
estimates.moderator_quote: participants were categorized into four exposure groups: Unexposed (0), Mildly exposed (1–2), Moderately exposed (3–4), and Highly exposed (5–7).
estimates.notes: Stricter threshold variant of the at-least-one row (same sample, same instrument, higher cut-point).

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; self-reported onward sharing of narratives, asked in an online survey
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who reported having shared at least one of seven political disinformation narratives
estimates.denominator: 3,240 Czech-speaking adults aged 16+ in a quota-balanced national online panel
estimates.definition: Respondent answered that they had shared at least one of the seven presented disinformation narratives (dummy yes/no across the seven items)
estimates.misinfo_def: “information that is (i) false, (ii) communicated as true, and (iii) intentionally communicated as true in order to influence people’s beliefs or behavior” (Kwek et al., 2023)
estimates.source_quote: Sharing behavior. Across the entire sample, only 10 % of participants (N = 310) reported sharing at least one disinformation narrative.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Narratives selected by media experts as real, circulating Czech disinformation; sharing itself is self-reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: A dummy variable (yes/no) was established to categorize all participants based on whether they shared at least one disinformation narrative out of seven which were presented.
estimates.notes: Paper rounds to 10 %; the exact part/whole is 310/3240 = 9.6 %. Observed (retrospective) self-report of actual sharing, not a hypothetical sharing intention.

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; self-reported onward sharing of narratives, asked in an online survey
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who had encountered at least one disinformation narrative who reported sharing ALL the narratives they had encountered
estimates.denominator: 2,131 respondents who reported encountering at least one of the seven disinformation narratives
estimates.definition: Respondent reported sharing every disinformation narrative they said they had encountered
estimates.misinfo_def: “information that is (i) false, (ii) communicated as true, and (iii) intentionally communicated as true in order to influence people’s beliefs or behavior” (Kwek et al., 2023)
estimates.source_quote: Among those who had encountered at least one disinformation item (N = 2131), the majority (86 %) did not share any, while 3.2 % (N = 68) reported sharing all the disinformation narratives they had encountered.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Narratives selected by media experts; sharing self-reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: for participants, which reported to previously encounter at least one disinformation narrative (i.e., had an opportunity to share disinformation), the ratio of disinformation (0–100 %), which were shared was computed.
estimates.notes: Conditional-on-exposure variant of the sharing row; denominator is the exposed subsample, not the full sample. The complementary 86% who shared none is not extracted separately (it is the complement of the same split).

estimates.platform: Not platform-specific; self-reported onward sharing of narratives, asked in an online survey
estimates.measure_type: Mean % of the disinformation narratives a respondent had encountered that they reported sharing
estimates.value_raw: 8.2 % of the recognized disinformation narratives (SD = 22.4 %); mean 0.18 items shared (SD = 0.70)
estimates.denominator: Disinformation narratives recognised by respondents (mean of within-person share-of-encountered ratios)
estimates.definition: Per respondent, number of encountered disinformation narratives reported as shared divided by number encountered; averaged across respondents
estimates.misinfo_def: “information that is (i) false, (ii) communicated as true, and (iii) intentionally communicated as true in order to influence people’s beliefs or behavior” (Kwek et al., 2023)
estimates.source_quote: On average, participants shared 0.18 disinformation items (SD = 0.70), corresponding to 8.2 % of the recognized disinformation narratives (SD = 22.4 %).
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Narratives selected by media experts; sharing self-reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: the ratio of disinformation (0–100 %), which were shared was computed
estimates.notes: This is a MEAN OF WITHIN-PERSON RATIOS, not a pooled share of items; it is reported verbatim as a percentage so it is kept, but it is not comparable to an item-level share and should probably be treated as a secondary/appendix estimate. Denominator scope coded 'population' because the underlying design is a survey.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) All trust/credibility results (33.3% trusted no disinformation narrative; 4.6% trusted all; 'nearly 20 % trusted disinformation more'; Table 2 trust means; discernment scores) — belief in false claims is explicitly out of scope. (b) Mean number of narratives recognised (1.60 of 7, SD 1.67) — a mean count, not a share of respondents; converting it to 22.9% would be a computed value the paper never states. (c) Sociodemographic subgroup shares (men 9.0% vs women 10.1% shared at least one; 53% of 16-24s unexposed; sharing proportion 13.4% elementary vs 3.7% university; 'approximately one third of the oldest participants (>65) were at least moderately exposed') — demographic subgroups, not the paper's headline, and the headline full-sample figures are already captured. (d) 'some disinformation narratives (e.g., G and A) were encountered by more than one-third of participants, others (e.g., F and C) by fewer than 12 %' — per-narrative exposure rates are given only as ranges/thresholds without the narrative-level numbers (full table is in unavailable supplementary Table S15); a range_not_point row would add nothing beyond the at-least-one row. (e) Factual-news exposure and sharing figures (39.3% recognised none; 5.6% shared at least one news item) — true content, not misinformation. (f) Predicted sharing probabilities from logistic models (>20% for narratives B and C when trusted) — model-predicted, not observed shares.

rob.design: Quota-balanced national online panel (Czech-speaking, 16+), balanced on age, gender, education, region, settlement size, internet use, occupational status and voting behaviour; 3,994 invited, 3,480 entered (response rate 87.1%), 40 excluded on quota, 130 incomplete, 70 excluded for short completion time, final n = 3,240. Stimuli were seven real disinformation narratives plus three fact-checked true news items chosen by media experts and presented as plain text without source attribution, in randomised order. Exposure and sharing were binary self-reports per narrative. No inter-rater reliability for narrative selection is reported; Cronbach's alpha = 0.815 / McDonald's omega = 0.819 is reported for the disinformation TRUST scale only. Study is exploratory and not preregistered; authors note self-reported exposure is subject to recall bias.
rob.item6_quote: The disinformation items were chosen using the following criteria: (a) their demonstrable presence and popularity in Czech online media and social networks, (b) their potential to polarize public opinion, and (c) their thematic relevance to dominant political discourses (e.g., Russian aggression in Ukraine, EU regulation, US military presence in Czechia). All selected disinformation narratives represented real examples of misinformation or disinformation that had been actively circulating in the public sphere.
rob.item10_quote: Across the entire sample, only 10 % of participants (N = 310) reported sharing at least one disinformation narrative. Among those who had encountered at least one disinformation item (N = 2131), the majority (86 %) did not share any, while 3.2 % (N = 68) reported sharing all the disinformation narratives they had encountered.
